editorNote: EXTRA EDITION: The portable-computer pioneer that once seemed unstoppable seeks bankruptcy protection, while a new generation of truly lap-size machines and inventive games points ahead.
morningLine: Osborne falls, Electronic Arts plays on, and portable computing sheds twenty pounds.

milestone.title: Osborne Computer declares bankruptcy
milestone.note: The September 13 filing ended the first great success story in portable personal computing and became the industry’s enduring warning about announcing replacements before they are ready.

lead.headline: OSBORNE CRASHES INTO BANKRUPTCY
lead.dek: The portable pioneer seeks Chapter 11 protection after demand collapses and suppliers are left owed $45 million.
body: SAN FRANCISCO — Osborne Computer sought bankruptcy protection September 13, a stunning reversal for the company that turned a suitcase-sized computer and a rich software bundle into one of personal computing’s first spectacular success stories.

The 24-pound Osborne 1 sold for $1,795 with a five-inch display, 64 kilobytes of memory, a modem, two 5.25-inch floppy drives, and software valued at roughly $1,500. The formula drove sales to about $70 million in 1982 and made “portable” a serious category rather than a laboratory curiosity.

But customers stopped buying the Osborne 1 while waiting for the announced Executive successor. TIME reports monthly unit sales plunging from about 10,000 in February to roughly 100 in April. The delayed new machine failed to arrive in time to replace the evaporating revenue.

Manufacturing stopped early this month. Four hundred workers were laid off, Adam Osborne resigned, and only about 80 employees remained as the company entered filing week with virtually no income and $45 million owed to suppliers.

The failure offers a brutal lesson to every fast-moving microcomputer maker: a promised successor can destroy today’s product before tomorrow’s is ready. Osborne made portable computing visible; its collapse now makes timing, cash, and customer confidence just as visible.

stories.headline: Shakeout Reaches Computers and Cartridges
stories.dek: Victor cuts jobs, Adam slips again, and Imagic layoffs show the boom’s harsher side.
body: Osborne is not alone in feeling the market turn. TIME reports Victor Technologies has laid off 350 workers and expects a third-quarter loss, while Coleco’s $600-to-$700 Adam home computer has slipped again, putting its Christmas arrival in doubt.

The contraction reaches videogames too. A September 17 New York Times brief reports layoffs at Imagic, the prominent independent cartridge publisher. Hardware makers and software houses alike are learning that crowded shelves and ambitious forecasts cannot guarantee demand.
The surviving firms will need tighter inventories, dependable delivery dates, and products that stand apart in a market suddenly less forgiving of delay.

stories.headline: M.U.L.E. and Archon Turn Rivalry into Art
stories.dek: Electronic Arts’ first wave mixes strategy, arcade action, and face-to-face competition.
body: Electronic Arts is making a persuasive case that computer games can be a creative medium. Dan Bunten’s M.U.L.E. turns an Atari space colony into a four-player contest of land claims, production, auctions, and supply-and-demand economics.

Archon: The Light and the Dark begins like a fantasy chessboard, then lets opposing pieces settle captures through real-time combat. The combination makes tactical position and joystick skill equally important.

Both games place human rivals at the center. The Atari 400 and 800’s four joystick ports give M.U.L.E. a living-room immediacy that solitary adventures cannot match, while Archon converts every encounter into a miniature arcade duel.

stories.headline: A Portable That Really Fits the Lap
stories.dek: NEC’s battery-powered PC-8201 points beyond the 24-pound luggable.
body: September’s Personal Computing calls the NEC PC-8201 a “lap-size portable computer,” language that draws a sharp contrast with the Osborne 1’s 24-pound bulk.

Positioned against Tandy’s Model 100, the battery-powered NEC suggests the next portable market may belong in a briefcase and operate away from a wall socket. Portability is shifting from a handle on a heavy case to a machine that can travel as naturally as papers.
